Microsoft has identified the root causes of a global outage that crippled Outlook, Exchange, and other core office software last week. The company issued an initial report on Monday identifying three contributing factors: a months-old latent bug, malfunctioning internal connections, and reduced server capacity. Each factor alone may have been easily resolved, but together they produced a major disruption that was harder to mitigate, according to Microsoft executives.

The outage began Thursday with U.S. users reporting interrupted access to their Outlook email accounts. As it continued into the following day, millions of people worldwide lost access to email and other Office 365 services entirely. The impact extended across critical infrastructure: jails could not release prisoners, hospitals reverted to paper records, schools lost contact with parents, and police departments were unable to receive crime reports.

Charles Lamanna, executive vice-president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform at Microsoft, explained the technical sequence in a Monday post on X. He noted that the company normally maintains two available networking gateways serving as entry and exit points between systems. However, one gateway was not functioning for Microsoft Teams, which overwhelmed the primary gateway. Subsequently, over 14% of the company's server capacity became unavailable due to an unrelated issue from the previous day. Lamanna wrote that this combination of increased load and reduced capacity caused the network gateway to encounter the latent bug originating in July, leading requests to build up until servers ultimately stopped responding.

The disruption occurred during peak traffic windows in the United States. Recovery took longer than usual because returning servers were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and became unresponsive again; Microsoft's normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from such a broad state of unresponsiveness, and standard rollback mechanisms could not quickly revert the months-old defect.

Microsoft resolved the issue and restored service by Saturday, also issuing an apology. The company did not attribute the blackout to a cybersecurity breach. Analysts say the incident highlights the need for organizations to examine their reliance on single operating systems, with NCC Group's Matt Hull describing it as "a prime example of the importance of not only cyber resilience, but business resilience," noting that widespread impact across essential services demonstrates how severe an outage can be regardless of cause.
items.title: Microsoft Attributes Global Outage to Months-Old Bug Combined with Gateway and Capacity Failures

items.summary: At Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World conference Monday, OpenAI Chief Financial Officer Sarah Friar said Anthropic's IPO is good for the ecosystem and good for us, adding that OpenAI was unconcerned with being second. She noted retail investors are ready for access to frontier models beyond hyperscalers, which come with pros and cons. After OpenAI closed a $122 billion fundraise in March this year, Friar said the company is closing out a smaller fundraise at a $1.25 trillion valuation. But she suggested the latest round was unplanned and opportunistic, prompted after a well-respected publication announced they were fundraising when they weren't — which caused inbound investor interest, leading OpenAI to move quickly in about a six-week period with completion by the midterms. Friar also said OpenAI's advertising model has been very successful, garnering more than $1 billion in revenue under 200 days, a record for the company. Addressing public resentment over data centers, she said companies must show up in communities and be accountable to regain trust; in Georgia, where OpenAI is building a 3.2 gigawatt data center, it has sponsored school lunches, a local park, and an AI summit for small businesses. Yet Friar acknowledged OpenAI still faces backlash from the AI buildout evident in US midterm elections, noting people are bombarded by rage that makes them feel they should react — but face-to-face engagement yields different conversations and outcomes.
items.title: OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar on Unplanned Fundraise, Advertising Success and Data Center Trust Issues

items.summary:
When a massive outage struck Microsoft late last week, much of the digital world ground to a halt. The disruption wiped out key services including Outlook, Teams and Copilot, which are used by more than 430 million people around the world. As email and internal communications froze, governments and businesses went dark alongside them, triggering an economic paralysis that could cost billions of dollars. While the global economy absorbs the brunt of this paralysis, Microsoft faces both a severe reputational hit and contractual penalties that could reach up to US$800 million per day for services it failed to deliver.

The initial source of Microsoft’s failure was incredibly innocuous: data centres usually share user demand across systems worldwide, but last week a small configuration change caused the company to lose control of some computers. Unable to share the load, these machines dropped requests onto other systems, overwhelming them and producing more outages in a repeating pattern until the company lost almost complete control of its network. Worse still, disconnected devices – phones, email clients and business systems – all tried to reconnect at once, crashing Microsoft’s systems repeatedly.

Historically an outage might affect only a single company, but Microsoft’s reach came down to a business revolution that silently took place over 20 years ago: the shift from selling software for upfront costs to renting access through “software as a service.” This transition shifted power toward tech companies and locked consumers into highly expensive long-term contracts. The global financial crisis in 2008 introduced too big to fail, when banks became too systemically important to be allowed to collapse; unfortunately the world has not learned those lessons.

Instead of bailing out failing institutions as it did with banks in 2008, society now endures a slow-motion version of that dynamic with tech. Centralisation, consolidation and unchecked monopolies have left digital lives, businesses and governments in an incredibly precarious place. Almost everything on the internet goes through Google, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon Web Services or CrowdStrike – all of which have had major outages over recent years.

Escaping reliance on a few tech giants has spurred the push for so-called digital sovereignty. Europe is leading the way by actively funding decentralised cloud infrastructure and homegrown software to ensure an American failure cannot knock out a local hospital, and Australia appears well placed to grasp these opportunities given its engineering talent – companies such as Atlassian, Apromore, Airwallex and Canva have already built world-class digital tools. Strategic investment in local tech ecosystems would provide not just digital insurance but also market competition, dilute big-tech monopoly power and spread systemic risks so a single point of failure could never bring the economy to its knees.

This is not to say we should divest from big-tech platforms entirely; they will continue providing useful services. But if our global economy keeps relying on a handful of too-big-to-fail digital monopolies, we will have no one but ourselves to blame when screens inevitably go black again.
items.title: Commentary: Microsoft outage shows that big tech can’t be treated as too big to fail

items.summary: South African President Cyril Ramaphosa told Semafor on Monday that Elon Musk’s “difficulty in understanding” a key South African policy is the main issue preventing his Starlink satellite internet service from launching in Africa’s biggest economy. Under the country’s Black Economic Empowerment (BEE) policy, introduced nearly 30 years ago to redress apartheid-era inequality, at least 30% of the South African operation of any company must be sold to Black locals — a requirement Musk has called “openly racist” and cited as the reason Starlink does not operate in the country. Ramaphosa countered that all countries have policies governing how they admit companies to operate, insisting one “has got to subscribe to the policies of the country.” He added that Musk “doesn’t fully understand the extent” of apartheid’s impact on Black South Africans and should be loyal to the nation where he spent his early years. The interview also touched on broader US-South Africa tensions: Ramaphosa described an Oval Office meeting, in which Trump accused him of presiding over a white genocide, as an “ambush,” calling Trump “seriously misinformed” and noting that this widely discredited belief underpinned Washington’s approach to South Africa. The two leaders have not spoken since the meeting. Ramaphosa said Musk has been influential in American politics and business since Donald Trump began his second term in January 2025, including helping shutter USAID as a government adviser, and that this influence contributed to friction between Washington and Pretoria — which South Africa has refused to reform BEE over and previously angered by its criticism of Israel. Separately, Ramaphosa said he was in California meeting tech executives, with talks planned for OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, and Google; when asked about opposition to data center buildouts worldwide, he noted that South Africa welcomes them.
items.title: Elon Musk’s policy difficulty prevents Starlink’s South Africa entry

items.summary:
In opening remarks at the Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference hosted by the Federal Reserve Board and the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco in November 2026, Chairman Warsh reflected that this was his first visit to a Reserve Bank as Chairman. He praised the gathering's forward-looking spirit and framed central banking as team sport serving the mission of 'One Fed. Fit for Purpose. Focused on the Future.' Warsh credited Marc, Chad, and Asha with leading the task force, noting their insight, experience, and willingness to think hard about what might come next.

The remarks then turned to a personal connection: Warsh arrived in California as a Stanford undergraduate in 1988, recalling Green Library during his freshman year Thanksgiving break. He described the Bay Area at that time as neither boom nor bust—a quieter period between tech surges—and expressed continued eagerness to learn from capable minds around him.

Warsh identified 'super intelligence' (SI) as an entirely new force in economic life and society, arguing it demands special attention because its marginal cost of satisfying curiosity is falling fast. Drawing on endogenous growth theory, he noted that ideas are the ultimate resource: while costly to discover, they are free to use and nonrivalrous, so their value grows with adoption. Citing Nobel laureate Paul Romer, Warsh observed that a doubling of ideas can more than double output through increasing returns to scale.

However, Warsh cautioned that over the past several decades breakthrough ideas have grown harder to find—even as research efforts increased more than 20 times since the 1930s. Nick Bloom and coauthors reported that 'Research productivity has fallen by an even larger amount,' while long-run growth also depends on population dynamics; slower population growth had prompted many economists, in Warsh's account, to return to secular stagnation themes.

Warsh then posed whether SI might change this picture, suggesting it could supercharge idea generation and sustain growth above the long-run average—though he insisted humans remain irreplaceable as designers, builders, and deciders. He invoked economist Bob Mundell's observation that the rise of the United States as a superpower was 'the most important fact of the twentieth century,' reframing American leadership today as an ongoing charge rather than mere history.

Warsh made clear his colleagues are not futurists or predictors; their job is contingency planning for risks that could be highly disruptive and economically costly, especially to critical infrastructure. He identified three big questions about magnitude, scope, and timing: whether SI raises total factor productivity, whether democratized knowledge lifts living standards, when the surge begins and tapers, and whether adversaries will race to deploy it harmfully.

Warsh acknowledged that while he is not here to offer predictions, he is 'not exactly impartial about American leadership.' He recalled a collaboration with mentor John Cogan at the Hoover Institution, quoting their vision of America's bright future. The Board's staff has begun evaluating illustrative—not forecast—scenarios: one in which SI broadly shared gains and real GDP growth rises persistently above average; others involving labor market disruption or disappointing returns that could slow the economy and raise unemployment before eventual recovery.

The finalized table captured only two labeled quantity meanings—the research-effort increase 'more than 20 times since the 1930s' (quantity-3861-3869) and Romer's doubling relationship ('doubling of ideas...can more than double output', quantity-4017-4018). No digit-written quantities were missed by the table, as all substantive measured quantities in the text are either dates or page/line citations from footnotes. The named_mentions list correctly identified organizations (Federal Reserve entities), people (Warsh, Mary, task force leaders, Romer, Bloom et al.), and places (San Francisco conference venue, Stanford, Green Library, Bay Area).
items.title: Chairman Warsh's Opening Remarks on Super Intelligence and Fed Preparedness

items.summary: This NBER Working Paper by Philip DeCicca, Harry Krashinsky, and Erik T. Nesson examines the growing electoral divide between men and women voters over roughly 40 years of American political history. While male and female support for both major parties was comparable in 1980, more recent surveys reveal a gap of about 10 to 15 percentage points in Democratic party preference among women relative to men. The authors attribute this divergence primarily to compulsory schooling laws (CSLs) and their effect on educational attainment, arguing that the timing of political polarization coincides with changes in these laws—particularly in states where CSLs had a stronger impact on average education levels. In those high-impact states, shifts in schooling requirements and resulting educational gains explain nearly all of the diverging party support and differences over major policy issues such as gun control and abortion by sex.
items.title: Compulsory Schooling and Gender Voting Polarization in U.S. Party Preferences

items.summary: Luca Gagliardone, Mark Gertler, Simone Lenzu, Joris Tielens, and Al-Mahdi Ebsim derive an aggregate state-space representation of state-dependent pricing models that incorporate random menu costs and strategic complementarities. The representation is built from first principles: it replaces the cross-sectional distribution of price gaps with a finite set of its moments—specifically the first three—while preserving the key economic forces of state-dependent pricing, namely movements in the frequency of price adjustment and selection. Along the impulse response, inflation emerges as an odd (cubic) polynomial in the average price gap. Embedded in a general equilibrium setting, the model can be solved by perturbation, filtered, and estimated with standard DSGE tools, and it matches well the global solution across shock sizes. Applied to the 2021–22 inflation surge in the United States and the euro area, the study shows that much of the variation which linear models would attribute to cost-push shocks is instead endogenous amplification through the frequency of price changes and selection.
items.title: An Odd Approximation of Inflation for State Dependent Pricing Models

items.summary: The article addresses young people aged 16-24 who are not in education, employment or training (Neets), noting that nearly one million fall into this group. A major review is expected to guarantee job placements or training for under-25s to help them secure permanent work. Across the whole economy there were 691,000 jobs available in July to September of this year, the lowest number since early 2021; stripping out pandemic fluctuations, vacancies are at their lowest level for 12 years. Apprenticeships remain a common entry into employment: in England the number starting apprenticeships aged 24 and under reached 172,230 in 2025, down from a peak of 291,300 in 2012, with growth driven largely by those aged 25 and over after schemes for older workers were fully rolled out in 2008. To locate suitable jobs, online adverts were analysed to identify vacancies appropriate for young people relative to local population size; South Oxfordshire had the most at 387 per 1,000 18 to 24-year-olds, while Rotherham had the least at 53 per 1,000. Data for London is available only as a whole region and not broken down by individual councils. On sectors, teaching led with the highest average number of entry-level vacancies in the year to October (mostly teaching assistants, learning support and cover supervisor roles), followed by hospitality and catering, then accounting and finance; this analysis was drawn from jobs website Adzuna, which includes full-time roles marked as entry-level, positions asking for up to two years' experience, graduate roles, internships and apprenticeships. Regarding pay, only about 40% of Adzuna's data for the year to October stated a salary, with figures varying widely by sector; average salaries were £30,530 in engineering (highest) and £25,880 in social care (lowest). Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently urged businesses to publish salaries ahead of plans to make pay details compulsory in adverts. The Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) think tank used AI to help identify the entry-level jobs.
items.title: Young Workers and Jobs: Vacancies, Apprenticeships, Entry-Level Sectors and Pay

items.summary:
In Vancouver—a city long among those with some of Canada's highest house prices—Elizabeth and Tom Wilcox, who have two children, found they could not afford the home they wanted. Their budget stood at C$1m (about $700,000 or £500,000), which would have secured only a small apartment with a balcony at best. Desperate for a house with a back garden large enough to fit a trampoline in a walkable neighbourhood, Elizabeth devised an idea: find another couple with young children and propose sharing the cost of a property so both families could move in together.

After placing an advert in a local estate agent's e-newsletter, it took two years before they met Ashley Pullman and her husband and two children—a family who clicked with them. In 2023, the Wilcoxes and the Pullmans co-bought a six-bedroom detached house with a back garden for C$1.85m. The families split the deposit of C$250,000 and continue to share the monthly mortgage payments of C$3,900 equally, dividing bills and other expenses—including home repairs—evenly as well.

Elizabeth says the arrangement has saved both families "tens of thousands of dollars." While there is no official data on how many people are buying homes with strangers, Parimal Gosal, founder and CEO of Husmates—an app and website connecting Canadians seeking to buy a home with someone they don't know—says he has seen a big increase in interest in Toronto amid high property prices. He describes the arrangement as "a financial relationship" that takes emotions out of it.

David Hollingworth, from British mortgage broker L&C, says although he hasn't encountered this himself, he believes it also occurs in the UK—though is "very niche." He recalls a pre-Covid matchmaking event in a London pub styled like speed dating for people wanting to buy a house with a stranger; how successful that was remains unknown.

Three years on, Elizabeth and Ashley say their living arrangement still works. While each family has private spaces such as their own kitchens, they share the basement-level living room—which includes a home gym in one corner and a shared freezer—and have never had issues over it. Ashley attributes her willingness to live with strangers partly to feeling like "the type of people who could live with strangers." Sabrina Bowman, a freelance business consultant in Toronto, has co-owned a home with two other housemates since 2018; when she moved in, she didn't know one of them. Though she is not comfortable sharing exact financial details, they divided the deposit and mortgage payments based on each person's income level.

Bowman stresses that household disputes can be addressed early through open discussion, noting: "What is important to us is having structures to communicate about everything that happens in the home." Her group holds regular house meetings covering chores, finances, birthdays and disagreements. She says it is valuable when people are honest about uncomfortable topics so solutions can be found.

For both Sabrina's Toronto home and the Wilcox-Pullman property in Vancouver, legal agreements exist in case someone wants to sell up and move out. Reasonable notice periods are specified for both; additionally, at Sabrina's home, a departing housemate must give the others first opportunity to buy their share. Tanya Walker, a Toronto real estate lawyer, says such legally binding assurances are vital rather than relying on messy emails or Facebook messages that could be lost if a dispute arises.

Back in Vancouver, Elizabeth notes neither family has set a timeframe for how long they will live in the house—all are happy with the setup and location, making it hard to move. She recalls the joy of watching her children jump on the trampoline for the first time or run around their patch of green grass.

The article does not provide official figures on the prevalence of this arrangement elsewhere in the world, acknowledging that its commonality beyond Canada remains unclear.
items.title: Canadian families co-buy homes with strangers to cope with unaffordable housing prices

items.summary: China aims to lead the global artificial intelligence race but recognizes it requires cutting-edge chips, prompting Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang—who chairs the Communist Party's Commission on Science and Technology—to strengthen domestic technological innovation as a strategic counterweight to the United States. China is deploying AI for surveillance, advanced unmanned weapons systems, robotics, and industrial automation. The US has long led in manufacturing technology and chip design, taking measures to preserve its dominance; since 2023, the Biden administration restricted exports of advanced semiconductors and chip-making equipment on national-security grounds, though Beijing condemned these as unilateral and arbitrary while many US chipmakers remained drawn to China's large market. Jensen Huang, who resigned last week as CEO of Nvidia amid revelations of extramarital relationships—including one with a businesswoman suspected by the US of spying for Beijing—had previously pushed for looser restrictions on selling AI chips to China; in December the Trump administration permitted Nvidia to ship its H200 chips provided Washington received a 25% cut, and each chip carries a price tag of $27,000 (€24,000), with demand estimated at 2 million units worth roughly $5.4 billion from this product alone. Beijing denied any attempt to ensnare Huang, calling the spying allegations unsubstantiated and a smear campaign, while stepping up rhetoric ahead of President Xi Jinping's meeting with Trump at this week's APEC summit in Shenzhen; Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on November 13 that China opposes misuse of export controls threatening global supply chains. Domestic debate intensified: Global Times questioned the affair's relevance to China and accused US media of turning it into a melodrama, while Weibo users attributed Huang's downfall to political maneuvering within the United States—underscoring an underlying economic calculation over whether China should rely on US chips or back its domestic industry. Currently around 600,000 Nvidia H200 chips sit in Hong Kong awaiting Chinese import approval despite White House authorization; Karson Elmgren of the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy noted this suggests China does not treat short-term advantages as decisive and remains confident it can replace US chips over the medium term. Chinese AI products increasingly use domestically made chips, which Tiantian Wang of Harbin Institute of Technology argued mitigates cyberattack risks by foreign actors; she emphasized that strengthening autonomy over national defense and critical infrastructure has become central to China's security strategy—citing radar systems in Chengdu J-20 fighter jets and Dongfeng-41 intercontinental ballistic missiles as equipped exclusively with Chinese chips—and highlighted a closed ecosystem spanning data, algorithms, computing power, and chips. Yet China still lacks production equipment for state-of-the-art chips: ASML has halted exports of its most advanced lithography machines to Beijing under Washington pressure, though the Center for Technology & Statecraft warned that additional imports in 2024-2025 could enable Chinese annual output sufficient to erode or even surpass US lead. According to Deloitte, China is planning extensive investments shifting from supporting individual companies toward fostering supply-chain synergies and ensuring secure management of critical resources.
items.title: Nvidia Scandal: China's Chips Dilemma and US Rivalry Shape AI Race

items.summary:
Nvidia's board is not considering reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO, according to three people familiar with the matter. This stands despite a growing campaign for his return that emerged days after affairs involving employees and suspected Chinese intelligence ties forced his resignation from the role.

The momentum behind restoring Huang has been substantial: more than 180,200 people have signed a petition demanding his return to leadership. High-profile figures have joined the effort, including Elon Musk, who threw his support behind it, and U.S. President Donald Trump, who said he would not mind seeing Huang reinstated as CEO.

Thousands of individuals identifying themselves as Nvidia employees have also participated in calls for Huang's comeback, even though governance experts and some investors caution that bringing him back before investigations are complete could expose the company to fresh risks.

The groundswell of support has transformed what began as a corporate succession story into a broader test of whether Nvidia can separate itself from a founder whose influence extends across its employees — some fiercely loyal to the former CEO — and shareholders, Silicon Valley, the Taiwanese supply chain, and Washington.
items.title: Nvidia Rules Out Huang Comeback as Campaign for His Return Grows

items.summary:
President Donald Trump said on Monday that he “would not mind” if Jensen Huang returned to lead Nvidia, following the executive's turbulent exit last week amid a scandal involving multiple extramarital relationships—one with Alice Huang of Megaspeed—an alleged Chinese spy connection, and an investigation into whether Beijing obtained sensitive U.S. technology. Trump told reporters he believes the founder of the world’s largest chipmaker “learned a big lesson,” that national security “was not put at risk,” and that he does not know whether Alice Huang was a spy.

Trump's remarks add to a growing chorus backing Huang's return, including an online petition with more than 175,000 signatures from figures such as Elon Musk of SpaceX and Tesla, Amjad Masad of Replit, and Tim Sweeney of Epic Games. A “Stand With Jensen” campaign letter endorsed by Nvidia employees, allies, shareholders, and supporters demands that the Board bring Huang back while an independent investigation establishes the facts.

Huang resigned last week as the board weighed his departure amid a scandal over multiple extramarital relationships involving Alice Huang, to whom Nvidia sold billions of dollars’ worth of advanced chips. U.S. officials say Megaspeed's actions could have endangered national security; Beijing has denied the allegations, and it has not been formally revealed that Megaspeed violated export rules.

The Trump administration was briefed on the matter but reportedly downplayed the issue amid its close ties to Huang, according to The New York Times. Bloomberg reported that during the probe Nvidia was asked to review shipment destinations to Megaspeed, which had imported about 50,000 more chips than found in its data centers.

The scandal has hit Nvidia's shares and cast doubt on future sales deals for a firm crucial to the AI race. The Financial Times reported that Huang told associates he was considering a possible return but has not spoken publicly about it. A group of Silicon Valley executives is seeking White House support, though his potential return could create tensions within the Trump administration.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent aired differences with Commerce Department colleague Howard Lutnick over how U.S.-sensitive technology exports such as Nvidia chips were handled. Washington Democrat Maria Cantwell criticized the commerce secretary for not preventing China from obtaining advanced chips, writing in a letter dated November 15 that “America cannot maintain its leadership in AI if the agency responsible for protecting that advantage fails to enforce its own controls.”

A little more than a year ago, The New York Times reported authorities were investigating whether Megaspeed helped Chinese customers obtain Nvidia chips subject to Washington's export controls. After Tuesday's market close, Nvidia is scheduled to release quarterly results—the first without Huang at the helm and with CFO Colette Kress serving as interim chief.
items.title: Trump Says He 'Would Not Mind' If Jensen Huang Returns to Nvidia

items.summary:
President Trump is traveling to Asia this week for a high-stakes trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin, marking his second visit to China in as many years. The trip coincides with widespread backlash from voters following the recent midterm elections, which may weaken his bargaining position across the Pacific. Tech billionaire Elon Musk is joining Trump in Shenzhen this time around.

The president's administration faces scrutiny amid the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who admitted an extramarital affair and was reportedly recruited by China's top spy agency—though NPR has not independently confirmed those reports. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick agreed to appear before the Senate Banking Committee to answer further questions.

Expectations for major deals or pronouncements from the meetings are low, but officials anticipate the summit will still make waves over its imagery. Discussions of Iran war and denuclearization with Putin and Xi may be limited; former CSIS adviser Edgard Kagan noted China likely won't want to engage on nuclear weapons given concerns about subservience and precedent. A White House official described the trilateral meeting as an "entry point" for reducing nuclear stockpiles, though no agreement is expected.

Russia's war with Ukraine nears its five-year mark, but there are no plans for a separate Putin-Trump meeting—though Trump said he would discuss his "favorite subject," Ukraine. Before China, Trump will first travel to the Philippines for meetings at the ASEAN summit in Manila, including talks with Quad nations India, Japan and Australia.

The president is expected to be in the region for just about three days. This marks the second time Trump and Xi have met on the sidelines of an APEC summit—but this year's differs from last year's meeting in Busan, South Korea, when tensions were high amid a trade war that established a fragile truce.

Former Asia Group managing partner Kurt Tong expects the agreement to be renewed past its January expiration, likely either in Shenzhen or at the G20 summit Trump is hosting in Miami. The Manila meetings offer an opportunity for Trump to repair relationships with allies like Japan and India before facing scrutiny over his party's loss of Congress.
items.title: Trump heads to Asia amid Nvidia fallout for trilateral summit with Xi and Putin

items.summary:
The United States announced tighter restrictions on exports of advanced semiconductors to certain countries—including Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil—requiring a licence for any export, re-export or in-country transfer. The US said these nations present a higher-than-normal risk of illegally diverting the chips to China, as part of broader efforts to limit China's access to top AI chips from companies like Nvidia. Under the rules, the licence requirement does not apply to semiconductors destined for companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent is headquartered in the US, provided certain reporting requirements are met.

In response, Singapore’s Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry (METI) and the Ministry of Digital Development and Information (MDDI) said on Tuesday that they were carefully studying the details of the new measure. The two ministries stated they were engaging affected companies to understand potential business impacts, consulting relevant US authorities on the scope and implementation of the rules, and exploring ways to facilitate trusted access for Singapore-based companies. They emphasized that Singapore takes its international reputation seriously and does not condone firms using their association with the country to circumvent or violate other nations' laws—including export controls.

The US move coincides with an ongoing investigation into Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud company and Nvidia partner accused of possible illegal diversion of chips to China. Allegations emerged that Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang aided at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip shipments to China. Alice Huang, a Hong Kong resident and former executive who served as then-CEO, chairperson and one of the key controllers of Megaspeed, was investigated for suspected involvement in possible offences relating to inaccurate declarations during the purchase of servers.

In February 2026, after consulting the Attorney-General's Chambers, police concluded there was insufficient evidence that Huang committed any such offences. However, she was barred from re-entering Singapore because authorities assessed that she knowingly provided inaccurate information to downplay her role in the company during investigations. Police investigations into Megaspeed and six other individuals remain ongoing.
items.title: Singapore assesses impact of new US chip export controls amid Megaspeed probe

items.summary:
The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim final rule targeting foreign remote access to advanced computing chips, including Nvidia's Blackwell. The measure addresses a growing concern that rapid advancement in cloud computing has made it increasingly possible for countries subject to export restrictions to reach the most advanced American AI capabilities remotely through data centers located outside their borders. Under former President Joe Biden and his CHIPS Act strategy—which bans sales of the most advanced chips to China—companies have been able to sidestep these restrictions by renting powerful hardware from overseas facilities in Southeast Asia rather than purchasing directly.

The new rule requires overseas data centers to conduct due diligence on customers, undermines their ability to use US chips to train advanced AI models, and places additional restrictions on those supplying significant volumes of computing power to companies headquartered in high-risk countries such as China, Russia and Iran. The provision goes into effect in 90 days and will require a license to export advanced chips to firms with headquarters in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil—nations the administration considers higher than normal risk for smuggling.

The move follows alleged spying connected to Nvidia, prompting US investigators to examine whether Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud company, helped Chinese clients obtain export-controlled Nvidia chips. Jensen Huang, Nvidia's co-founder who stepped down as CEO last week after admitting an extramarital affair with Alice Huang—a former Megaspeed executive suspected of spying for China—was central to the scrutiny. Megaspeed rejected allegations that it sent chips to China.

The rule comes just days before President Donald Trump is scheduled to travel to China for an economic summit, where he will meet his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping.
items.title: US Clamps Down on Chip 'Loophole' in Foreign Access to Advanced AI Chips

items.summary: Upmarket retailer David Jones collapsed into voluntary administration in early November after years of steep losses left the heritage chain falling behind on rent and supplier payments. Administrators McGrathNicol broke down a debt pile estimated at over $400m, including an estimated $180m owed to suppliers and $11m to employees, alongside about $33m in unredeemed gift cards held by shoppers and significant sums due to secured creditors such as the retailer's main financier Hilco. The administration followed accelerating financial losses and reputational damage that threatened its ability to stock shelves for Christmas; funding pressures coupled with damaged reputation were affecting its capacity to obtain stock for the trading period, with some suppliers reportedly owed money from goods sent back as early as April. David Jones recorded a net loss of $228m last financial year according to updated figures disclosed to creditors, and lost a further $69m in the first four months of the new financial year leading up to administration. Under a dual appointment, FTI Consulting has day-to-day control of operations while administrators McGrathNicol seek a buyer or fresh injection of capital; the retailer is set to shutter half of its 38 department stores by end of year under a sweeping restructure that would trigger mass job losses.
items.title: David Jones Collapses Into Administration Amid Debt Over $400m

items.summary:
Bank of England Governor Mark Carney warned that rising U.S. tariffs under President Donald Trump could drive Canadian automakers to look toward China if the North American auto market becomes less integrated. Speaking on Monday ahead of a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping at this week's APEC summit in southern China, Carney said Canada has "the best auto workers in the world" and wants them fully deployed within an integrated regional market.

Carney attributed the declining integration to U.S. trade actions, noting that the current system represents "the best result for Canadian workers, for Canadian business, and for US consumers." He emphasized at a summit of French-speaking nations in Cambodia that this arrangement was not leverage but rather "action, reaction"—a direct response to shifting conditions.

The backdrop includes Trump's punishing tariffs on Canada's auto sector imposed last year, alongside his repeated insistence that vehicles sold in the United States be made exclusively by American workers. Although Carney walked away from trade talks with Trump in August, Ottawa and Washington have expressed optimism about prospects for a deal in recent weeks. Should negotiations settle differently, Carney noted there would be other options available—European, Asian, Chinese, or Japanese.
items.title: Carney warns US tariffs could push Canadian automakers toward China

items.summary: China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC) announced on Monday that its longest carbon dioxide transmission pipeline was put into operation in northeast China's Jilin Province. The Jilin Petrochemical-Jilin Oilfield pipeline measures 277.6 kilometers in length and can transport up to 3.3 million tonnes of carbon dioxide annually, making it the country's largest CO2 pipe by diameter, pressure, and designed transportation capacity. The trunk line crosses three cities in Jilin Province—Jilin, Changchun, and Songyuan—and connects upstream carbon capture facilities at Jilin Petrochemical with downstream oil recovery and carbon storage operations at Jilin Oilfield. During construction, engineers achieved a series of technological breakthroughs and the domestic production of several key pieces of equipment. Ma Xiaohong, chief expert at Jilin Oilfield, noted that wind and solar power are being used to supply green electricity to the project, helping reduce carbon emissions throughout its lifecycle. CNPC is now using the pipeline as the backbone of a regional carbon capture, utilization and storage (CCUS) network. The supporting CO2 recovery project at Jilin Petrochemical, with an annual capacity of 800,000 tonnes, went fully into operation in October, providing stable supply to the pipeline.
items.title: China's longest carbon dioxide pipeline begins operations in Jilin Province

items.summary:
The APEC Ambassadors and CEOs Roundtable was held in Shenzhen, China on November 15, 2026. Hosted by the Finance Program Center of China Media Group (CMG), it took place during CMG's first major media event at the 2026 APEC Leaders' Week. The roundtable centered on the theme "Shared Open Opportunities for Win-Win Outcomes" and served as a platform for dialogue among Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation member economies and Chinese enterprises, marking what was described as the "Shenzhen moment" of China's designated APEC year.

A panel delivered remarks at the event. Shen Haixiong, deputy head of the Publicity Department of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and president of CMG, noted that the Asia-Pacific region is a powerhouse of global economic growth and expressed hope that the roundtable would deepen mutual understanding among partners and help build an Asia-Pacific community for common prosperity. Ren Hongbin, chairman of the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade (CCPIT), said China will uphold consistent, stable policies to advance high-quality development and high-standard opening-up, while CCPIT aims to unlock fresh opportunities for industrial cooperation across the region.

Foreign ambassadors shared their perspectives on bilateral ties. Djauhari Oratmangun, ambassador of Indonesia, credited China's investment, technologies and industrial expertise with boosting Indonesian growth and called for deeper collaboration between enterprises of both countries. Thaddeus Kambanei, Papua New Guinea's ambassador, thanked CMG for organizing the forum and described China as a key source of trade, investment and technology. Carlos Vasquez, Peru's ambassador, highlighted that an upgraded protocol to the China-Peru free trade agreement had recently entered into force, coinciding with the 55th anniversary of diplomatic ties between the two nations; he pointed to Chancay Port as a landmark of bilateral cooperation.

Ma Mingzhe of Ping An Group said the roundtable offered a rare channel for foreign diplomats and Chinese entrepreneurs to engage directly. Executives from leading firms including Gree, Hisense, Seres, EVE Energy, Hiconics and TCL exchanged views with ambassadors on high-standard opening-up and AI industrial development.

Around 80 participants attended the gathering, including officials from CMG and CCPIT, diplomatic representatives from APEC member economies, executives of Chinese and overseas companies, and representatives of foreign business associations.
items.title: APEC Ambassadors and CEOs Roundtable Held in Shenzhen

items.summary: Franklin independent Peter George has tabled a bill in Tasmania's parliament seeking a moratorium on new data centre developments until binding rules are established. The disclosure of his shares in Sydney-headquartered property giant Goodman Group drew attention because the company's global development pipeline is now almost 80 per cent focused on data centres, up from 57 per cent to 68 per cent by September last year and rising further to 78 per cent as it builds facilities for cloud and AI customers. In its full-year results released in August, Goodman Group reported that data centre development accounted for more than $15 billion out of a total $19.7 billion global work in progress — the two figures explicitly quantified in the article's finalized table. Mr George said his interest relates to Goodman's commercial buildings holdings rather than its data centre operations, and he would review his shares as the company changes portfolio listings. The Tasmanian government recently released an 'expectations' document for developers covering renewable energy partnering (without requiring new firming capacity if available from Hydro Tasmania), efficient water use, a community benefit fund, designated build zones, retained public consultation and appeal rights — but it was not binding. Labor leader Josh Willie criticized the approach as giving developers too much latitude with protections negotiated behind closed doors, while Premier Jeremy Rockliff defended the expectations, emphasizing getting 'the balance right.' The Tasmanian government's lack of specific planning controls remains a point of contention for Mr George amid community concerns about impacts on communities and natural resources.
items.title: Tasmanian MP Declares Goodman Group Shares as He Pushes Data Centre Moratorium Bill

items.summary: The article opens by observing that the U.S. dollar has long dominated Africa's financial landscape, establishing it as the established currency of the region. It then introduces a shift underway: as more African countries turn to China's yuan, the balance of economic power could be changing. The piece frames this transition not merely as a monetary swap but as a potential realignment in global influence, suggesting that growing adoption of the yuan may gradually erode dollar dominance across the continent.
items.title: Africa: Trading in yuan

items.summary: Late Monday night Russian attacks struck two major bridges in Kyiv as part of an overnight assault that damaged critical infrastructure and knocked out heating and water across parts of the capital, according to its mayor. The strikes came even as Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky had warned of a possible Russian attack in the coming days while negotiators representing Kyiv along with Europe and the United States held talks on future negotiations aimed at finding a path to end the war. Separately, Russia for the second day running hit a symbolic bridge linking the annexed Crimean peninsula to Russia, according to a Moscow-installed official speaking Tuesday. Zelensky also said intelligence indicated Russia was planning new strikes on Ukrainian targets Monday evening, overnight and into Tuesday, per a Reuters report. In related news, Russian President Vladimir Putin could meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un if he attends this week's APEC summit in China, Interfax quoted Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov as saying Monday.
items.title: Russian strikes hit Kyiv bridges amid war-end talks and Putin-Kim summit speculation

items.summary:
Russian forces struck two major bridges crossing the Dnipro River in Kyiv late on Monday, damaging critical infrastructure and causing water and power cuts in parts of the Ukrainian capital, according to Mayor Vitali Klitschko. The attacks came as Moscow launched a wider wave of drone and missile strikes across Ukraine, including in the regions of Cherkasy and Kharkiv. According to preliminary information reported by Klitschko on Telegram, there had been hits on the North and South bridges in the capital, along with some other critical infrastructure.

Reuters witnesses reported a series of loud explosions in the capital, though Reuters could not immediately independently confirm the reports. Russian forces launched a series of attacks on bridges crossing the river earlier this month and in October. In Cherkasy, a Russian missile attack injured three people, while Kharkiv was also targeted; local officials said these events occurred via Telegram.

Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians. President Volodymyr Zelenskiy had earlier that Monday stated intelligence showed Russia's military planned strikes for Monday evening and throughout Tuesday. On the same day, Ukraine hit a strategically important bridge and targeted oil refineries in what Russian defence ministry data described as the biggest overnight drone attack on Russia since the start of full-scale war in 2022.

The attacks continued overnight, with the Crimea Bridge being hit again while Moscow downed nearly 200 drones heading in its direction, according to Telegram statements. Zelenskiy also said Ukraine had held new online talks with US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, as well as European representatives, on prospects of ending the war that Russia started by invading Ukraine in February 2022.
items.title: Russian strikes hit two key bridges in Kyiv, disrupting water and power supplies

items.summary:
A new OpenAI study finds that 98 per cent of surveyed scientists expect artificial intelligence to accelerate discoveries in their fields, underscoring the growing role of tools such as ChatGPT in research. The findings draw on an analysis of 580,186 scientific messages from 1,819 researchers and a survey of 251 scientists using OpenAI's ChatGPT for Academic Researchers programme. Scientists estimate that AI lets them complete tasks at the same quality level in nearly half the time, with more than one in five believing a discovery normally taking 10 years could be achieved within three years. Reading and writing together accounted for more than half of the average scientist's messages, while AI was used across stages including reviewing literature, writing, analysing evidence, developing software, and generating research ideas.

The report notes that human involvement remains essential: researchers sought clarification, checks or revisions after around 32 per cent of AI responses. At the same time, bottlenecks persist — limited time or staffing was cited by 51.8 per cent of respondents as a constraint, while 43.8 per cent pointed to funding; only 6.4 per cent reported having no major bottlenecks. OpenAI said that translating productivity gains into faster discoveries will also depend on funding, staff and the capacity to conduct experiments.

The study was published November 17, 2026.
items.title: OpenAI Study: 98% of Scientists Expect AI to Accelerate Discoveries

items.summary: US stocks fell sharply on Monday amid a broad risk-off selloff triggered by the fallout from Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO. The chipmaker slid 4.1%, extending its losses after Huang departed following allegations of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, which soured enthusiasm for AI stocks and raised stakes ahead of Nvidia's earnings report on Tuesday and Anthropic's IPO later in the week.
items.title: Nvidia Slides as US Tech Stocks Plunge on Jensen Huang Resignation Fallout

items.summary: An estimate by market intelligence firm EIIR Trend, shared with Economic Times (ET), suggests that last week's Microsoft outage could have dealt a roughly $200 million hit to the Indian information technology services industry. The study estimates this against an overall sector size of about $315 billion for India's IT services industry. According to the cited analysis, the loss of connectivity through the affected enterprise suite left IT services companies facing lost billable hours, delayed project execution, and additional costs related to delivery commitments.
items.title: Microsoft Outage's $200 Million Billing Blow to India's IT Services Industry

items.summary: The article examines a category of fraud affecting Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions that extends beyond user error—such as sharing OTPs or scanning fake QR codes—to deeper device-level compromises. While awareness campaigns have long addressed careless mistakes like approving deceptive 'collect' requests, officials note that some frauds stem from chinks in existing security solutions where devices may be compromised at the underlying Android operating system level, outside the control of individual customer-facing payment apps known as third-party application providers. Vishwas Patel, chairman of Payments Council of India (PCI), described this as an 'App world issue,' stating that feedback has been sent to Google from many in the app ecosystem and expressing belief that Google is doing what it can to minimize frauds arising from malicious sideloading of third-party applications on Android.
items.title: NPCI, UPI apps turn to Google over Android security vulnerabilities enabling fraud

items.summary:
US intelligence indicates that Iran is developing contingency plans to potentially target senior Trump administration officials in Washington, DC, using a radioactive dirty bomb or chemical weapons. CNN reported this assessment quoting seven US officials familiar with the intelligence. The intelligence points to specific potential locations and targets in the US capital, prompting American authorities to step up contingency planning.

However, officials told CNN that the reported preparations do not necessarily indicate an imminent attack or a decision by Tehran to execute such a plot. One source described the preparations as “prudent,” while another noted that whether Iran has the personnel in place to execute is a matter of debate. Two officials said several meetings had been held over the past week to discuss measures to counter the potential threat.

The White House responded, saying it was monitoring potential threats but maintained there was no immediate credible threat to the US mainland. In a statement, spokesperson Lauren Bis said that “there are no credible threats to the homeland.” According to CNN, officials view the intelligence as possibly indicating Tehran is considering escalating conflict beyond the Middle East amid continued American military pressure and an economic blockade.

The reported concerns come against the backdrop of previous Iranian plotting against current and former American officials. Such activities have continued since Trump's first administration and largely focused on targeting US officials while travelling overseas, including an alleged murder-for-hire plot against Trump in 2024.

American intelligence agencies are also monitoring information suggesting Iran could consider using chemical weapons against US troops stationed in the Middle East. CNN reported that several officials have raised concerns that American troops may not have adequate protective equipment or training to respond to such an attack, prompting a separate contingency planning exercise focused on protecting diplomatic and intelligence personnel in the region.

The reported threats come as Washington and Tehran remain locked in a conflict centred around the Strait of Hormuz, with stalled diplomatic efforts yet to produce a breakthrough. Although regional sources believe both sides are interested in reaching an agreement, neither has appeared willing to make major concessions. A US official cautioned that if Iran's leadership begins viewing its regime's survival as at stake, it could consider taking risks that would otherwise be unacceptable.

The reported threat comes amid uncertainty over a key US surveillance law that allows authorities to collect communications involving foreign nationals. The law expired in June following a political standoff between the White House and Congress. Surveillance orders approved before its expiry remain valid until March 2027, but national security officials have warned that losing the provision could weaken their ability to identify potential terrorist plots.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and CIA Director John Ratcliffe wrote to Republican and Democratic leaders urging reauthorization. In their letter, they argued delays would “(put) the lives of both Americans in the homeland and our troops stationed abroad at risk.” The lawmakers had received a briefing on Iran several days before the letter was sent.

The Iranian Mission to the United Nations in New York rejected allegations involving chemical weapons but did not directly address the reported intelligence about a potential dirty bomb plot. In a statement, an Iranian spokesperson said Iran “considers the use of chemical weapons under any circumstances to be wholly illegitimate and categorically rejects” the false allegations.

A dirty bomb is a conventional explosive device designed to spread radioactive material over an area. Unlike a nuclear weapon, it does not rely on fission or produce a nuclear explosion. Although considerably less destructive than a nuclear weapon, it can disperse radioactive material and contaminate surrounding areas. The immediate casualties would generally result from the conventional blast, while radioactive material could create additional contamination risks.

A source familiar with the intelligence said “Any weapon like that is a weapon of terror, not a weapon of precision,” adding that they “can make people really sick and certain areas uninhabitable.” American officials believe acquiring radioactive material would be one of the main challenges in assembling such a device. The US intelligence assessment has also raised questions about the country's ability to detect potential plots before they are carried out.
items.title: Iran planning dirty bomb attack in Washington, US intel warns

items.summary: A senior Reserve Bank of India official reiterated the central bank's demand that Tata Sons, the holding company of the conglomerate spanning salt to software, be listed in accordance with existing regulations. A Deputy General Manager in RBI's Department of Regulation wrote a letter on Monday responding to a communication from Tata Sons Pvt Ltd dated October 6, advising compliance with all applicable rules governing non-banking companies in the upper layer, including listing requirements. The bank first pressed for a listing when it rejected Tata Sons' application to de-register as an NBFC on September 11, ahead of a board meeting on September 17 that surfaced divisions at the group's higher echelons. Noel Tata, half-brother of Ratan Tata and current chair of Tata Trusts—which owns over two-thirds of Tata Sons—opposes the listing, viewing it as a threat to the Tata way of working, while management led by N Chandrasekaran believes compliance with the law is necessary. Shapoorji Pallonji Group, the largest private owner in Tata Sons with an 18 per cent stake, supports a listing because it would help raise liquidity to clear its substantial debt.
items.title: RBI Reiterates Demand for Tata Sons Listing Amid Deepening Group Rifts

items.summary: In an interview with reporters in New Delhi on Monday, IBM chairman and CEO Arvind Krishna said the company is holding talks for at least two large projects in India beyond the Amravati Quantum Tech Park. He declined to name them until a signature was obtained and funding confirmed, but described them as serious ventures similar in structure to the first project, which took about two years to land properly.
items.title: IBM CEO Arvind Krishna on India Projects and Quantum Investment

items.summary:
The US Department of Commerce introduced new export controls on advanced semiconductors and overseas data centres, seeking to prevent companies linked to countries of concern from accessing significant computing power based on US technology. Under an interim final rule (IFR), the department is introducing restrictions on overseas data centres that remotely provide substantial computing capacity to companies headquartered in countries classified under Country Group D:5 or Macau. The move is aimed at preventing entities in these jurisdictions from using advanced US-made semiconductors to train sophisticated artificial intelligence models.

The rules also add licensing requirements for some advanced semiconductor exports and transfers, applying to exports, reexports and domestic transfers of advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil — countries Washington considers to present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. An exemption is available for shipments to companies headquartered in the US, or with US-headquartered ultimate parent companies, if they meet reporting requirements.

The measures come amid growing scrutiny of Nvidia and its CEO Jensen Huang following allegations that advanced AI servers powered by the company's chips were smuggled into China. In March, US authorities charged Super Micro Computer founder and two others with allegedly smuggling servers containing Nvidia chips worth $2.5 billion to China; the company itself was not named in the indictment but said it was cooperating fully with the investigation.

The latest regulations do not specifically target Nvidia or directly refer to the Megaspeed investigation, though they seek to address a broader vulnerability: access to advanced computing power through overseas infrastructure. Data centres, foreign chip fabrication facilities and chip exporters must conduct robust due diligence on customers, examining whether companies are directly or indirectly owned or controlled by individuals or entities based in restricted jurisdictions.

The licensing requirement will not cover commercial recommendation systems, including those used by online retailers and social media platforms, which the Commerce Department said do not pose the same national security risks. The interim final rule also formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden administration's AI Diffusion Rule — a framework BIS had announced its decision to rescind in May 2025 that was never enforced.

The broader shift indicates Washington is moving towards identifying potential diversion routes, scrutinising ownership structures and monitoring access to computing infrastructure. Potential consequences for countries that tolerate attempts to evade the new restrictions include import restrictions, additional licensing requirements, downgrading their status under the US export control regime, and placing foreign individuals or companies involved in evasion on the Entity List.
items.title: Nvidia chip row: US tightens AI chip export rules to restrict access through overseas data centres

items.summary: Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India and US President Donald Trump will participate in the Quad Leaders Summit held alongside the ASEAN-India and East Asia summits in Manila. This marks the first Quad meeting since September 2024, taking place during ongoing bilateral trade negotiations between India and the United States. The discussions are expected to cover supply chains, maritime security, critical minerals, and artificial intelligence across the Indo-Pacific region. The summit also underscores India's trade and cultural ties with Southeast Asia while supporting its Act East and SAGAR initiatives. Separately, the USS Roosevelt has joined two other US warships in West Asia, increasing military presence amid rising tensions with Iran following midterm polls. In unrelated political developments, Shobha De reviewed Sonia Gandhi's memoir as a readable but romanticized personal narrative lacking strong political insight, noting historical omissions and shifts in political blame; meanwhile, Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Vijay attended an event hosted by Sonia Gandhi alongside Karnataka CM Shivakumar amid tensions over the Mekedatu dam.
items.title: Modi and Trump to Attend Quad Leaders Summit in Manila Amid Trade Talks

items.summary: Prime Minister Narendra Modi arrived in Manila for the India-ASEAN and East Asia Summit meetings, stating that his visit would inject new energy into India's partnership with Southeast Asian nations and reinforce collective commitment to a peaceful, prosperous and resilient Indo-Pacific. Soon after landing, he attended a dinner hosted by Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr ahead of Tuesday's multilateral and bilateral engagements. Although no bilateral meeting with US President Trump had been scheduled as late as Monday evening, official sources confirmed the Quad leaders' summit would proceed that night; Modi was expected to return to India late on Tuesday. On Tuesday morning he attended a groundbreaking ceremony at a gurudwara before participating in the 23rd ASEAN-India Summit. In his departure statement from Delhi, Modi emphasized that India's relationship with ASEAN countries is central to its Act East Policy and occupies a key place within its MAHASAGAR vision, describing ties rooted in centuries of civilisational exchange as having grown into a dynamic partnership spanning trade, connectivity, maritime security, technology and people-to-people relations. He also expressed anticipation for building on the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership at the ASEAN-India Summit to advance shared aspirations for growth, connectivity and prosperity, while noting he would interact with the Indian community in the Philippines. Modi further highlighted the East Asia Summit as an important platform for dialogue on regional and global challenges. The Quad leaders' summit—described as the first such meeting since Trump returned to the White House—is expected to draw maximum attention in India and possibly Japan; amid speculation that Trump might have downgraded the Quad, it is anticipated to reaffirm commitment rather than announce fresh initiatives across shared interests including maritime security, critical technologies, supply chains, connectivity, health and economic security. The US framed its 'partnership of action' around peace, prosperity and security in the Indo-Pacific region. As Trump heads into a trilateral summit with Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping and Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, observers will watch whether he tones down Quad rhetoric on China or modulates messaging regarding the South and East China Seas.
items.title: Modi's Manila Visit: Asean Ties Central to India's Act East Policy Amid Quad Summit and Trump-APEC Travel

items.summary: On November 17, Brent crude futures fell 64 cents (0.7%) to $91.8 a barrel while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures dropped 55 cents (0.6%) to $85.17, continuing the week's declines of 16% and 13%, respectively. The benchmarks' softness reflects growing expectations that global supply will outstrip demand. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), average oil supply in Q4 would reach roughly 105 million barrels per day—about 1.7 million bpd above forecast demand, marking a shift from its earlier expectation of a fourth-quarter deficit as Middle East exports recover faster than global consumption despite ongoing attacks on shipping. Traders are now contemplating excess supply for the first time since the US-Iran conflict began, and analysts note that this narrative change is dampening market tone; KCM Trade's Tim Waterer observed that while the geopolitical risk premium from the US-Iran conflict has not vanished, it is taking a back seat as attacks on Gulf infrastructure and shipping in the Strait of Hormuz persist. Looking further ahead, Goldman Sachs expects Brent to average $88 a barrel next year before easing to $78 by end-2027 as supply disruption risks remain but the risk premium normalizes. Citing Goldman analysts including Daan Struyven via Bloomberg, crude supply is projected to exceed end-use demand by 2 million barrels per day in 2027 even after accounting for potential disruptions of half that magnitude. The brokerage's base case assumes Middle Eastern supply would rise above its 2025 average—supported by ship-to-ship transfers and pipeline additions—while production growth elsewhere stalls, leaving the market caught between elevated supply disruption risks and industry adaptability.
items.title: Oil Prices Ease as Supply Surplus Hopes Grow; Goldman Sachs Forecasts Lower Brent Through 2027

items.summary: Spot gold was little changed at $3,856.52 per ounce by 0028 GMT after hitting its lowest level since October 2025 on Monday. US gold futures for December delivery rose 0.2% to $3,859. Bullion sank to a one-year low on Monday, battered by high Treasury yields, a strong dollar and expectations of tighter monetary policy, putting it on course for further losses and its worst year in more than a decade. The dollar rose to its highest level since April 2025, supported by last week's strong inflation data and hawkish Fed commentary; a stronger dollar makes greenback-priced bullion more expensive for overseas buyers. Markets see a 96.6% chance of a 25-basis-point rate hike in December, while the probability of a larger 50-basis-point move is priced at 3.4%, according to CME's FedWatch tool. Elsewhere, Bank of Japan hawkish board member Hajime Takata said its policy rate must rise to a good position early and focus on mounting inflation risks, signalling a possible hike as soon as December. Among other metals, spot silver steadied at $47.05 per ounce, platinum gained 0.1% to $1,450.75 and palladium rose 0.1% to $969.75.
items.title: Gold Near One-Year Low as Strong Dollar and Fed-Hike Bets Weigh

items.summary: According to CNN, US intelligence has picked up reports that Iran is developing plans to target senior Trump administration officials by detonating a so-called dirty bomb or chemical weapon inside the United States. The report cited seven officials and said the plotting has been very specific, including locations and targets within Washington, DC. However, sources told CNN that these potential attacks represent options rather than an indicator of imminent threat, with no evidence suggesting Iran has decided to move forward; whether it even has personnel in place to execute such a plan remains debated. US intelligence views active planning for unconventional weapons on its own territory as a signal of alarming willingness to escalate by Iran. Officials feel the country is vulnerable to dirty bombs—devices that package radioactive materials into conventional explosives and can spread radiation across blocks or miles—which are easy to assemble and could be carried out by someone already living inside the US, exploiting porous borders over roughly ten years. The report came days after an Iranian diplomat on X threatened harm against two US Navy personnel blamed for a Tomahawk missile attack that killed more than 150 people, mostly students, in Minab on February 28 during the opening hours of the US-Israeli war.
items.title: US Intelligence Warns Iran Is Planning Dirty Bomb and Chemical Attacks on Trump Officials in Washington

items.summary:
Finshots explores how Indonesia can be rewarded for conserving rainforests even as those forests burn, framing the tension around palm oil. In 2022, Norway agreed to pay Indonesia up to $1 billion—$5 per tonne of deforestation emissions cut—for reducing such emissions from forest degradation; last week it announced roughly $90 million because between 2020 and 2023 Indonesia reduced those emissions by around 270 million tonnes of carbon dioxide. Yet simultaneously, at the COP31 climate summit in Turkey that opened last week, Indonesia sought international funding to protect its national forests even though over 70,000 hectares inside 47 national parks had already burned by September from forest fires.

The contradiction stems largely from palm oil demand. Indonesia is the world's largest producer of palm oil and needs more land for it; when prices fall, plantation owners have less incentive to clear additional forests. A 2022 study found a 1% drop in palm oil prices was associated with a 0.68% decline in forest loss. Another driver is Indonesia's B50 biodiesel mandate introduced last year, requiring diesel sold domestically to contain 50% biodiesel—largely from palm oil—to reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels and strengthen energy security.

Domestically, Indonesia already consumes a large share of its own palm oil: in 2024 it used 53% of total production under the older B35 mandate (a 35% blend). The shift to B50 could push domestic demand higher, leaving less for exports and supporting prices. This has consequences at scale—Indonesia doubled its oil palm plantation area between 2001 and 2019 to about 16 million hectares, and a recent study estimates meeting the B50 target by 2030 could require converting up to another 8.5 million hectares of land.

Peatland is especially at risk: Indonesia holds nearly one-third of the world's peatlands—waterlogged soil that stores enormous carbon as natural sinks, but where oil palms don't grow well because their roots rot in water. Plantation owners dig canals to drain it, exposing buried organic matter to oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide; the ground also subsides and becomes drier and more fire-prone. Estimates suggest peat subsidence alone released around 148 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent (or greenhouse gases) in Indonesia in 2024, and together with peat fires it accounted for nearly 85% of the palm oil sector's assessed emissions—worsened by El Niño conditions. This is where biodiesel's climate promise unravels: clearing lowland tropical rainforest to grow palms creates a carbon debt that scientists estimate would take around 86 years of using palm biodiesel to repay, during which it releases more greenhouse gases than fossil diesel; if the plantation replaces peatland rainforest, payback could stretch to around 420 years.

The piece then draws a parallel with India's ethanol blending programme aimed at reducing dependence on imported crude oil. As demand for ethanol rose from 1.7 billion litres in 2019-20 to a projected 12 billion litres in 2025-26, manufacturers needed more raw materials—sugarcane and corn—with corn's share rising from virtually nothing in 2021-22 to around 37% in 2025-26. This competition with poultry farmers for corn raised feed costs, pressuring egg and chicken prices; the Economic Survey 2025-26 flagged a shift toward corn away from pulses and oilseeds, which could deepen India's dependence on edible oil imports.

The government has begun adjusting its ethanol policy: for 2026-27 it asked oil companies to stop procuring ethanol made from sugarcane juice, sugar syrup or raw sugar, and cut the corn-based ethanol incentive from ₹5.79 to ₹2.79 per litre—though reducing one crop may simply increase demand for another. India is Indonesia's largest palm oil export market, so rising Indian preference for corn over oilseeds could boost edible oil imports while Indonesia's growing domestic biodiesel demand leaves less palm oil available for export; both countries seek energy security but risk unintended consequences.

Proposed solutions include intensifying existing cultivated land rather than expanding plantations—smallholders manage about a third of Indonesia's plantation area, so better seedlings could raise yields without more land—but replanting programmes have consistently fallen short. Making biofuel blending targets flexible when food crops are scarce or expensive is another option; India dropping sugar from ethanol this year reflects that idea. Finally, countries could look beyond food crops to used cooking oil, agricultural waste and crop residues.

The bottom line: energy security and food security cannot be treated as separate goals—a policy reducing imported-oil dependence while raising food prices or destroying forests creates new problems while solving the primary one. A plantation earns money from every harvest; a standing forest gets little financial reward for its carbon, water and fire prevention—so until those benefits carry a price, forests will keep competing with more profitable land uses.
items.title: Indonesia's Palm Oil Carbon Debt and India's Biofuel Tradeoff
